why:
D4, from both sides. An extension `fun Slug.tidy()` is a **free function under the package module** — `java:shop.text.tidy`, never `java:shop.text.Slug.tidy` — because the receiver type does not own it; attaching it would hang a CONTAINS edge off a type that in real code usually lives in another module or in the SDK. The call side has to agree: `slug.tidy()` looks exactly like a member call and must still resolve to the free function. The plain top-level `shorten(slug)` is here as the contrast — same module-level id, no receiver.

**The imported half.** §6 assigns this case "an extension with the same name imported from elsewhere; the imported one is a hit only when its import is explicit", and the fixture had no import at all — so the half of the rule that actually breaks was never exercised. `shop.remote` now declares two extensions on the same receiver: `trim`, which `Ext.kt` imports explicitly, and `tidy`, which it does not. `slug.trim()` must therefore resolve to `java:shop.remote.trim` — a free function in *another* package, reached only because the import names it — while `slug.tidy()` keeps resolving to the same-file one, because a file's own declaration wins over a namesake it never imported.

refusals.why: PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING. `slug.tidy()` is syntactically a member call, so attaching the extension to its receiver type is the one tempting fabrication in Kotlin (D4, risks §11) — it reads naturally and is what a Java-trained reader expects. `Slug` does not declare `tidy`; the package does.

PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING, and it was happening. The same fabrication one file further out: an extension imported from another package is written exactly like a member call, and the per-file extension table only ever held *this* file’s, so the call fell through to the receiver type and produced `Slug.trim` — losing a grounded target for an invented one. The existing D4 test covered only the same-file half.

excluded: `Int` and `Long` are Kotlin builtins, not declarations of this repository, so neither gets a node and neither receiver can be checked against anything — the calls resolve because nothing contradicts them, which is the whole of the rule.
`n.scaled()` and `big.scaled()` are two call sites and one labelled edge: they name the same id, and the graph holds facts rather than occurrences.
